criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Cover memo identifies LTC ratio exceeds 80% maximum
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly identifies the LTC exceedance in multiple places. Section 3.1.1 states 'Loan-to-cost is 83.77% against an 80% maximum (Term Sheet §6.1), an excess of $2,140,000.' Issue A-2 is dedicated to the LTC exceedance, and Table 3 explicitly shows the recomputation '47,500,000 ÷ 56,700,000 = 83.774%' with the result 'exceeds the 80% maximum.' The top-risk register (Table 2, item 1) also flags the LTC breach as Critical. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Cover memo notes mezzanine loan doesn't count as borrower equity
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum identifies the $9,200,000 mezzanine loan, including through Brightleaf Mezzanine Capital LLC, and repeatedly states that mezzanine debt is borrowed money rather than borrower equity. It explains that if the land or budget was mezzanine-funded, the Borrower has no true equity and the LTC/LTV analyses rest on a false premise. It also directly ties the lack of borrower equity and the $47,500,000 senior loan to the 83.77% LTC breach.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Cover memo quantifies equity shortfall (~$2,140,000)
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum explicitly quantifies the equity/LTC shortfall as $2,140,000 in the Executive Summary (§3.1.1), in the top-risk register (Item 1), in Table 3 (LTC excess = $47,500,000 − $45,360,000 = $2,140,000, with the maximum loan at 80% LTC of $56,700,000 shown as $45,360,000), and in Issue A-2, which analyses the shortfall in detail and explains why the proposed $2,140,000 escrow does not cure it. The calculation matches the criterion precisely.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Loan agreement includes equity escrow or restructuring mechanism
criteria_results.reasoning: The agreement contains multiple operative mechanisms addressing the LTC gap: Section 2.6 requires the Commitment to be permanently reduced or cured by the Borrower funding additional equity sufficient to satisfy the 80% LTC (and 65% LTV) condition before Closing, with a Compliance Certificate five Business Days before Closing; Section 7.6 establishes a $2,140,000 Equity Deposit Account with equity-first application to Project Costs, source verification, and Commitment reduction if sourced from prohibited sources; Section 4.1(p) makes the Equity Deposit a condition precedent to the Initial Advance; Section 5.1(i) makes equity disbursement a condition to each Advance; and Section 6.3(c) requires the Borrower to deposit funds for cost overruns. Drafting Note 2 further analyzes that the escrow alone does not cure LTC unless the Commitment is reduced dollar-for-dollar, and Section 2.6 adopts exactly that restructuring. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Cover memo identifies interest reserve may be insufficient
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly flags the interest reserve adequacy issue. Table 2 (row 10, issue A-7) identifies the $4,850,000 interest reserve, notes the Borrower's claimed $221,325 surplus at 3.50% SOFR versus a $365,830 shortfall at 4.35% and the Credit Memo's ~$565,000 shortfall, and recommends re-modeling and increasing the reserve to approximately $5,215,830. Part 5, section A-7 provides detailed analysis showing the reserve may be insufficient over the 30-month construction period, with shortfalls reaching $1,278,000 at 5.35% and $9,025,000 interest on a full draw. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Cover memo notes below-market SOFR assumption in budget
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly identifies the below-market SOFR assumption in the interest reserve analysis. Issue A-7 states that the Borrower's Interest Reserve Analysis models a $221,325 surplus 'at an assumed SOFR of 3.50% (all-in 6.75%)' and contrasts it with the same sheet's sensitivity table showing a $365,830 shortfall at SOFR 4.35%, which the table annotates as 'Current market SOFR as of Jan 2025.' Table 3 likewise records the 3.50% assumption and cross-references the 4.35% current-market figure. The discrepancy is flagged and characterised as an understated assumption requiring re-modelling at current SOFR.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Loan agreement requires borrower to fund interest reserve shortfalls
criteria_results.reasoning: The loan agreement contains multiple provisions expressly addressing interest reserve insufficiency. Section 7.2 requires the Borrower to pay any shortfall when the Interest Reserve is insufficient. Section 7.3 prohibits replenishment from Loan proceeds and requires any replenishment 'from the Borrower's own funds.' Section 7.4 establishes an Interest Reserve Adequacy Test required with each Draw Request (and before each Advance), obligating the Borrower to deposit any deficiency before funding. Section 7.5 requires the Borrower to deposit funds within five (5) Business Days after notice of a projected deficiency, imposes quarterly adequacy assessments, and makes failure to deposit an Event of Default. Section 5.1(h) also makes the interest reserve test a condition to each Advance, and Section 3.7 requires the Borrower to pay interest from its own funds once the reserve is exhausted. Both the shortfall-funding requirement and a periodic (per-draw/quarterly) adequacy testing mechanism are clearly present.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Cover memo identifies conflicting pledges of membership interests
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly identifies the conflicting pledges in Issue D-1 ('Both loans are secured by a pledge of 100% of the membership interests and no intercreditor agreement exists'), citing Term Sheet §1.4 (mezzanine pledge of 100% of membership interests), Term Sheet §8 (senior pledge of 100% by all members), and the organizational chart, and states that 'Two first-priority pledges of the same collateral cannot both exist.' The issue is also escalated in the Executive Summary's Top-Risk Register as item 9 ('Competing 100% pledges; no intercreditor (D-1)'). Issue D-3 identifies the mezzanine lender as Brightleaf Mezzanine Capital LLC (an affiliate of the 28% member, Brightleaf Investors Group LLC), so the conflict is tied to the specific mezzanine lender named in the criterion. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Cover memo recommends intercreditor agreement as closing condition
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly recommends that execution of the intercreditor agreement be a hard, non-waivable closing condition and that the senior lender's pledge receive first priority. Issue D-1 states that the mezzanine pledge and senior pledge both purport to cover 100% of membership interests and that the intercreditor agreement is 'negotiated but is not yet executed'; the recommendation is to 'Make execution of the intercreditor agreement on the Credit Memorandum's terms a hard closing condition (not waivable); require the senior pledge to be perfected by delivery of certificates...'. The Top-Risk Register (item 9) likewise recommends 'Senior first, mezzanine second under a fully executed Intercreditor Agreement', and Part 14.2 lists D-1 among the non-waivable items. Draft §4.1(q) makes it a closing condition. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Loan agreement conditions closing on executed intercreditor agreement
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's draft expressly makes closing/initial advance conditional on the Intercreditor Agreement. Section 4.1(q) requires execution and delivery of the Intercreditor Agreement between the Lender and the Mezzanine Lender as a condition to the Initial Advance, and Section 14.5(a) further provides that no Advance may be made unless the Intercreditor Agreement is executed, delivered, and in full force. Article 14 also resolves the competing pledge priority by providing that the Lender's Liens rank first and the Mezzanine Lender's pledge ranks second under the Intercreditor Agreement. Thus the criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Cover memo identifies NFA residential use restriction conflict
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum identifies the NCDEQ NFA letter's restriction of approximately 0.38 acres to non-residential use, specifically discusses the northeast corner of Parcel 0821-04-72-4102, and flags the conflict with the project plans' 14 residential units above that restricted area in issue C-3 and related sections. It treats the issue as material, discusses whether the restriction is legally permissible, and recommends closing conditions and NCDEQ confirmation.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Cover memo discusses impact on appraised value and leasing
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly addresses the financial and valuation impact of the NFA residential use restriction. It discusses that 14 residential units may not be deliverable or leasable for residential use, quantifies the potential NOI loss at $377,160, states the resulting NOI of $4,499,640 and DSCR of 1.21x, and explains that the appraisal's as-completed and as-stabilised values ($72.8M and $76.2M) rest on the full 212-unit programme. It also recommends an appraisal addendum addressing value without the affected units. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Loan agreement includes environmental compliance covenant or CP
criteria_results.reasoning: The loan agreement extensively addresses the NFA residential use conflict. Section 4.1(e)(vi) is a condition precedent requiring, before closing or before advances for work above the Restricted Area, either (A) a written NCDEQ modification of the NFA Letter permitting residential use, (B) written NCDEQ confirmation that residential occupancy subject to the vapor mitigation system is permitted, or (C) a Lender-approved redesign eliminating residential use above the Restricted Area. Section 13.2(b) is an ongoing covenant prohibiting any use other than non-residential use of the Restricted Area unless NCDEQ modifies the NFA Letter in writing and the Lender consents. Section 13.4 requires an architect overlay analysis and satisfaction of those alternatives before residential units can be delivered, and Section 16.1(k) makes failure to comply with NFA Letter conditions an Event of Default. Environmental representations (8.1(n)) and NFA compliance covenants (13.1-13.5) are also included. This squarely satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Cover memo identifies borrower has zero direct cash equity
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum explicitly identifies that the Borrower's cash equity contribution is zero. Section 3.1.4 states that if the Borrower's budget is correct 'there is no equity in the capital stack.' Section A-3 states that Total Project Costs of $56,700,000 are funded by $47,500,000 of senior debt and $9,200,000 of mezzanine debt, 'with Borrower cash equity of zero (Term Sheet §5.1).' Table 3 shows Total Sources as '47,500,000 + 9,200,000 + 0.' The zero equity issue is therefore flagged and tied to the arithmetic specified in the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Cover memo discusses circular affiliate funding concern
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum extensively discusses the circular affiliate funding concern. Issue D-3 is devoted to it: Brightleaf Investors Group LLC (a 28% member) received its interest for $0 cash 'in consideration of its commitment to arrange third-party mezzanine financing,' which was arranged through Brightleaf Mezzanine Capital LLC — an entity under common control of Thomas R. Chen, who also manages Brightleaf Investors Group. The memo analyses the consequences (same economic interest on both sides of the senior loan, negative control over major decisions, affiliate subordinated lender, arm's-length concerns) and recommends disclosure, intercreditor protections, independent manager and non-consolidation opinion. Issue D-4 reinforces this by analysing the 'circular funding' of the land via mezzanine proceeds/member capital calls and noting the Credit Memorandum itself raised circular funding as a possibility. A-11 and E-7 also address the resulting invalidity of the equity analyses.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Loan agreement requires evidence of equity contribution as CP
criteria_results.reasoning: The draft contains an express condition precedent to closing requiring evidence of the Borrower's equity contribution: Section 4.1(p) ('Equity Contribution') requires evidence that the Equity Deposit ($2,140,000) has been made and that the source of funds has been verified under Section 7.6(c), which itself mandates traced capital call notices, subscription agreements, 90-day bank/brokerage statements and a managing member certificate, and provides for a dollar-for-dollar Commitment reduction if the equity is sourced from the Mezzanine Lender or affiliates. The draft also squarely addresses the adequacy of the land contribution as equity: Schedule 3 line 1.01 treats the $8,200,000 land acquisition as funded by the Mezzanine Loan, and Drafting Note 9 flags the three irreconcilable accounts of how the land was funded, warns that if the land was mezzanine-funded the 'land as equity' premise underlying LTC/LTV/HVCRE is wrong and combined leverage is 100%, and points to Sections 7.6(c) and 14.6 as protections; Drafting Note 16 further computes net land equity (~$5,500,000) against the $8,900,000 as-is value less the $3,400,000 existing mortgage. Annex I items 3 and 19 cross-reference these conflicts. The criterion is therefore satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Cover memo identifies unsatisfied prior deed of trust
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly flags the Triangle Commercial Bank deed of trust. Section 3.1.2 of the Executive Summary states that 'The $3,400,000 existing deed of trust is not funded anywhere in the sources and uses,' noting that the Title Commitment makes satisfaction of the Triangle Commercial Bank deed of trust (Book 6215, Page 892) a condition to issuing a first-priority policy. Issue B-2 is devoted to it, recording the Title Commitment Schedule B-I Requirement 4 (deed of trust dated September 14, 2018, securing $3,400,000 in favour of Triangle Commercial Bank) and recommending a payoff letter, inclusion of the payoff as a use, and simultaneous recording of the cancellation with the new Deed of Trust at or before closing (Draft §§4.1(h), 14.3). Table 2 ranks it as the #2 risk ('Existing Mortgage unfunded — Critical'). The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Loan agreement requires payoff/release of prior DOT as CP
criteria_results.reasoning: The agreement expressly makes payoff and release of the Triangle Commercial Bank deed of trust a condition precedent to closing. Section 4.1(h) requires evidence of satisfaction/discharge of the Existing Mortgage, including a recorded cancellation or certificate of satisfaction or the payoff amount held in escrow, sufficient to delete the title exception. Section 14.3 further requires the Existing Mortgage to be satisfied and discharged on the Closing Date, with the Title Company instructed to record the cancellation/certificate of satisfaction simultaneously with the Lender's Deed of Trust. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Cover memo identifies SPE/affiliate substantive consolidation risk
criteria_results.reasoning: Section D-3 of the cover memorandum expressly identifies that Brightleaf Investors Group LLC holds a 28% membership interest for $0 and that the mezzanine financing was arranged through Brightleaf Mezzanine Capital LLC, an entity under common control of Thomas R. Chen. The analysis explicitly links this affiliate relationship to substantive consolidation risk, noting the Credit Memorandum §9.3 identifies the risk and that 'the same economic interest sits on both sides of the senior loan.' D-5 further requires a non-consolidation opinion and independent manager to address this risk. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Cover memo recommends SPE protections (independent directors, non-consolidation opinions, anti-commingling)
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly recommends SPE protections, including appointing an independent manager and obtaining a non-consolidation opinion (Issue D-5), and further recommends independent-manager and non-consolidation protections in connection with the affiliate relationship (Issue D-3). This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Loan agreement includes SPE covenants addressing affiliate separation
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 12 of the draft contains comprehensive SPE and separateness covenants expressly addressing affiliate separation: Section 12.2(a) requires separate books, records, accounts and financial statements from any member, manager, Affiliate or the Mezzanine Lender; Section 12.2(b) prohibits commingling of funds with members, managers or Affiliates; Section 12.2(f) requires fair and reasonable allocation of shared overhead and arm's-length relationships with members, managers and Affiliates; Section 12.2(g)/(j) bar pledging assets or making loans to affiliates; and Section 12.4 requires an independent manager with approval rights over bankruptcy actions and organizational amendments. Section 12.5 adds non-consolidation opinion and annual separateness certification, and Events of Default in Section 16.1(i) enforce the SPE covenants. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Cover memo or loan agreement includes SOFR fallback/benchmark replacement
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.3(d) of the draft, captioned 'Benchmark Replacement,' expressly addresses the discontinuation or non-representativeness of SOFR, including triggers (permanent/indefinite discontinuation, administrator or regulator public statement, illegality of use), a mechanism for the Lender to substitute a successor benchmark rate with a conforming spread adjustment, reference to ARRC recommended best practices and prevailing market convention, thirty days' notice, and a 'hardwired' replacement requiring no Borrower consent provided the successor rate and adjustment are consistent with ARRC recommended fallback language and applied consistently to comparable CRE loans. This constitutes a benchmark replacement/conforming changes mechanism consistent with ARRC recommendations, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Cover memo identifies need for SOFR benchmark replacement provisions
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum addresses SOFR transition in section F-2, noting the Term Sheet's ARRC-consistent benchmark replacement provisions, that the benchmark replacement language is described but not drafted, and recommending hardwired replacement language along with lookback and related conventions. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Cover memo discusses completion guaranty
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum discusses the completion guaranty as part of the guaranty structure. Section 3.2 expressly refers to 'the completion and carry guaranties' alongside guarantor support as supporting the credit. Issue E-2 analyzes the Completion Guaranty in detail (noting it would be breached on the day given because the Construction Maturity Date precedes substantial completion, and recommending conforming the Completion Guaranty to an extended maturity date). The Completion Guaranty is also referenced in issues B-6 and E-3, and the Carry Guaranty is discussed in A-7. Thus the completion guaranty is clearly part of the memo's discussion of the guaranty structure.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Cover memo discusses 25% partial repayment guaranty at $11,875,000 each
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly discusses the 25% partial repayment guaranty and the $11,875,000-per-guarantor formulation. Under issue A-5, it records that the Term Sheet states an aggregate 25% guaranty of $11,875,000, while the Credit Memorandum states '$11,875,000 per guarantor,' and it analyzes the resulting discrepancy. The criterion is therefore satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Cover memo addresses need for bad boy carve-out triggers
criteria_results.reasoning: The criterion requires the cover memorandum to address 'bad boy' carve-out triggers (e.g., fraud, voluntary bankruptcy, unauthorized transfers, environmental liability) that would convert the partial repayment guaranty to full recourse. Reviewing the memo, the guaranty discussion is confined to quantum (A-5: $11,875,000 aggregate vs. 'per guarantor'), guarantor support/liquidity (H-1), and North Carolina anti-deficiency enforceability (H-2). Bankruptcy risk is discussed only in the structural/SPE context (D-3 affiliate-controlled bankruptcy risk; D-5 independent manager and non-consolidation opinion) — i.e., preventing a voluntary filing rather than triggering full recourse under the guaranty. Neither 'bad boy,' 'carve-out,' nor any trigger converting the partial guaranty to full recourse appears anywhere in the memorandum; there is no discussion of fraud, unauthorized transfers, or environmental-liability springing recourse. The criterion is therefore not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Loan agreement or guaranty provisions include bad boy carve-outs
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 15.1(e) of the draft expressly provides 'Recourse Carve-Outs' to the Partial Repayment Guaranty, stating that upon triggering events — including fraud or intentional misrepresentation, voluntary bankruptcy or insolvency filing by the Borrower, unauthorized transfer or encumbrance of the Property or Pledged Interests, environmental liability, waste, breach of SPE covenants, and failure to maintain required insurance — the Partial Repayment Guaranty converts into a full recourse obligation of each Guarantor for 100% of the outstanding principal balance, accrued interest, fees and enforcement costs. This matches the criterion's requirements for bad boy carve-out triggers converting a partial guaranty to full recourse, and the carve-outs are also cross-referenced in the guaranty provisions of Section 15.3 (continuing guaranty, waiver of defences, absolute and unconditional obligations).

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Addresses NC foreclosure considerations for guaranty
criteria_results.reasoning: The output squarely addresses North Carolina-specific foreclosure considerations relevant to the guaranty in both documents. The cover memorandum's Issue H-2 ('North Carolina's anti-deficiency regime affects the guaranty structure') analyzes N.C.G.S. § 45-21.16 (power-of-sale foreclosure notice/hearing) and § 45-21.36 (fair-value credit on deficiency judgments), and recommends a savings provision preserving the fair-value credit, a severability clause specific to the guaranties, a guarantee of payment without purporting to waive § 45-21.36, and a NC enforceability opinion. The loan agreement implements this: Section 15.3(e) expressly states the Guaranty is not discharged by foreclosure, deed in lieu, a deficiency judgment, or application of N.C.G.S. § 45-21.36; Section 15.4 ('Deficiency and Fair Price Confirmation') addresses the judicial foreclosure regime, § 45-21.16, and § 45-21.36, and confirms no non-waivable rights are waived; Section 17.4 ('Preservation of Anti-Deficiency Rights') restates the point in the remedies article. Drafting Note 19 further flags the election-of-remedies and waiver-enforceability questions. This comfortably satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Cover memo identifies unspecified extension option conditions
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo identifies in issue D-6 that the Term Sheet's six-month extension is 'subject to conditions to be set in the Loan Agreement' (i.e., to be determined without enumeration). It further recommends in issue A-10 (and Table 2, issue 3) a specific combined debt-service coverage test as a condition to any extension, implemented in Draft §21.2(d). This satisfies the criterion by flagging the unspecified extension conditions and establishing a specific condition for the drafter.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Loan agreement specifies at least 4 extension conditions
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 21 expressly enumerates at least four extension conditions, including no event of default, substantial completion and certificate of occupancy, minimum occupancy threshold, DSCR based on actual NOI, extension fee, interest rate cap, and continued effectiveness of the intercreditor agreement. All listed criteria are satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Cover memo or loan agreement addresses retainage release and NC lien law
criteria_results.reasoning: The loan agreement expressly ties retainage release to North Carolina lien law. Section 5.9/6.6/6.7 (Release Conditions for the Final Advance releasing the full $3,475,000 retainage, and noting the $3,275,000/$200,000 discrepancy) conditions the release on: (i) final, unconditional statutory-form lien waivers from the Contractor and each subcontractor and materialman, or, where no waiver is delivered, expiration of the statutory period for filing a claim of lien under N.C.G.S. §44A-12 without a claim being filed, or posting of a lien bond or other security acceptable to the Lender and Title Company (§6.7(c)); (ii) expiration of the Chapter 44A lien filing period or a title date-down confirming no liens filed (§6.7(d)); and (iii) a title date-down insuring the Deed of Trust free of claims (§6.7(e)). Article 4.1(m) also requires pre-closing statutory waivers and a lien agent designation under §44A-11.3, and Schedule 4 shows the retainage release as Advance 9. The cover memorandum likewise addresses retainage (issue E-3) and mechanic's lien relation-back/Chapter 44A risk (B-11). Thus retainage release is fully connected to lien waiver and lien-period requirements, satisfying ISSUE_011.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011: Loan agreement retainage release conditions include lien waivers
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 6.7 (Release Conditions) expressly requires architect's final completion certificate, final unconditional certificate of occupancy, final unconditional lien waivers from the contractor and subcontractors/materialmen (or expiration of the statutory lien period or posting of a lien bond), and expiration of the statutory lien period or title date-down confirming no liens. This satisfies the criterion by including at least two of the specified conditions, including lien waiver requirements.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Cover memo identifies CC&R architectural review as potential delay risk
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memorandum expressly identifies the Brightleaf Historic District Association's CC&R architectural review process as a potential construction-delay risk. Issue B-5 (Table 2 item 13) explains that the Appraisal assumes ARC approval, the title officer has no evidence of submission, and the Declaration requires submission at least 90 days before construction with the building permit conditioned on approval or deemed approval — so the City cannot issue a permit and construction cannot lawfully begin, making the 90-day period critical to the timetable. Issue B-6 adds that an unapproved exterior change could halt construction via the Association's injunctive rights, and recommends Lender consent to any plan change requiring ARC approval. Issue E-9 and A-6 reinforce that historic-district architectural review can force design changes and create schedule risk. The recorded book/page for the Declaration (Book 6984, Page 1155) is not cited — the memo refers to it via Title Commitment Exception 11 — but the substance of the criterion, identifying CC&R architectural review as a delay risk, is clearly met.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_012: Loan agreement requires evidence of CC&R/design approval as CP
criteria_results.reasoning: The draft expressly includes the CC&R/design approval requirement as a closing condition precedent in Section 4.1(k), which requires evidence that the Brightleaf Historic District Association Architectural Review Committee has approved the Approved Plans, or that the 60-day deemed-approval period has expired without written action, or a written waiver. It also includes covenant provisions requiring compliance with the recorded declaration and Architectural Review Committee approval: Section 9.1(q) (Architectural Review Compliance), Section 20.3 (submission of plans, obtaining approval or deemed approval, payment of assessments), Section 6.4(c) (change orders requiring ARB approval before Lender consent), Section 6.4(a) and 10.1(h)-(i) (plan modifications require Lender consent), and Schedule 2 Exception 11. Drafting Note 22 and Annex Item 17 flag the source-document inconsistency and confirm the requirement.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement correctly states loan amount as $47,500,000
criteria_results.reasoning: The draft states the Loan Amount consistently as $[47,500,000] — on the cover page, in Section 1.1(xx) ("'Loan Amount' means $[47,500,000]"), in the Commitment definition (Advances not to exceed the Loan Amount), in the Note (original principal amount of the Loan Amount), and in Schedule 3 (senior Loan column totals $47,500,000). Although the figure is bracketed as a working-draft item and Section 2.6 flags a possible LTC-driven reduction to $45,360,000, the agreement does state the maximum loan amount/commitment as $47,500,000. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement correctly identifies Lender as Pinnacle Savings Bank, N.A.
criteria_results.reasoning: The loan agreement consistently identifies the Lender as 'Pinnacle Savings Bank, N.A., a national banking association' — in the cover page header, in Section 1.1(uu) definition of 'Lender', in the signature block, and in the notice address block. The Lender is neither misnamed nor omitted.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement correctly identifies Borrower as Harborview Capital Partners LLC
criteria_results.reasoning: The loan agreement explicitly identifies the Borrower on the cover page as 'Harborview Capital Partners LLC, a North Carolina limited liability company,' and consistently names it as the Borrower throughout the document (e.g., Section 1.1(pp), Section 8.1(a), and signature block).

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement states construction period rate as Daily Simple SOFR + 3.25%
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.1 (Interest Rate — Construction Period) of the draft Loan Agreement expressly states that from the Closing Date through the last day of the Construction Period, the outstanding principal balance bears interest at a rate per annum equal to Daily Simple SOFR plus 3.25% (the 'Construction Rate'). The benchmark (Daily Simple SOFR), spread (3.25%), and per annum rate structure all match the criterion, and Section 3.3 further confirms the Daily Simple SOFR convention and 360-day year computation.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement states SOFR floor of 1.00%
criteria_results.reasoning: The loan agreement expressly defines a SOFR Floor of 1.00% in the definition of 'SOFR' and in Section 3.3(c). Section 3.3(c) states that if Daily Simple SOFR is less than 1.00%, SOFR shall be deemed to be 1.00% for determining interest, and it notes the resulting minimum all-in rate during the Construction Period. Since Section 3.1 applies Daily Simple SOFR plus 3.25% during the construction period, the 1.00% SOFR floor applies during construction.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement states correct mini-perm interest rate
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.2 states that during the Mini-Perm Period the Loan bears interest at 'Daily Simple SOFR plus 3.50%' (the 'Mini-Perm Rate'). The SOFR floor of 1.00% is specified in the definition of 'SOFR' (Section 1.1(ttt)) and in Section 3.3(c), which also confirms the resulting minimum all-in Mini-Perm rate of 4.50%. The rate, spread, and floor all match the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement states correct default rate
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 1.1(v) defines the "Default Rate" as the sum of (i) the rate of interest otherwise applicable to the Loan on such day under Section 3.1 or 3.2, plus (ii) five percent (5.00%). Section 3.4 applies that Default Rate upon an Event of Default, and Drafting Note 3 reiterates that the Default Rate is the applicable contract rate plus 5.00%. The 5.00% premium matches the criterion exactly.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement states correct construction maturity date
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 1.1(q) defines the Construction Maturity Date as [August 28, 2027] — exactly 30 months after the anticipated February 28, 2025 Closing Date — and the Construction Period is defined as commencing on the Closing Date and ending on that date. The date is stated correctly; the bracketed alternative (December 31, 2027) is a flagged drafting issue about schedule buffer and does not make the primary stated date incorrect.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement states correct mini-perm maturity date
criteria_results.reasoning: The agreement defines the Mini-Perm Maturity Date as August 28, 2028, which is 12 months after the stated Construction Maturity Date of August 28, 2027. This satisfies the criterion, though it also notes an alternative construction maturity date subject to drafting resolution.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement includes the 6-month extension option
criteria_results.reasoning: Article 21 includes a one-time Extension Option extending the Mini-Perm Maturity Date from August 28, 2028 to February 28, 2029, which is a 6-month extension as required by the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement states correct origination fee
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.5(a) states: 'The Borrower shall pay to the Lender at Closing a non-refundable origination fee of $475,000, being one percent (1.00%) of the Loan Amount.' This matches the criterion exactly—1.00% of the $47,500,000 Loan Amount ($475,000), payable at Closing. The amount is also consistently reflected in Schedule 3 (line 4.02, $475,000) and in the Initial Advance allocation in Section 5.5.

criteria_results.title: Loan agreement includes exit fee of 0.50% during construction period
